hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to sharp, high-contrast linear edges or elongated cylindrical structures oriented diagonally across the visual field. The activating features are consistently rendered as dark objects—typically deep black, charcoal, or dark grey—set against a uniform, lighter background of pale grey, white, or low-saturation monochrome tones. The specific visual form varies from thin metallic rods, cables, and wires to shadow boundaries, text alignment lines, and anatomical contours, provided they maintain a distinct linear profile. The neuron exhibits invariance to object identity, texture (responding to both smooth metal and grainy paper), and the specific direction of the slope (activating for both ascending and descending diagonals), as long as the high contrast and oblique geometry are preserved. The linear feature typically traverses a substantial portion of the frame, often spanning 50–90% of the image width or height, and is frequently oriented at an angle of approximately 25–30 degrees relative to the horizontal.
